analysis.one_liner: Requires people's consent before companies sell their personal information, financial records, health data, or Social Security numbers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in January 2005, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped companies from selling or sharing a person's name, address, phone number, or email for marketing without notice and a chance to say no. It would have made it a crime to display, sell, or buy someone's Social Security number without their consent, banned printing Social Security numbers on government checks and driver's licenses, and rewritten the financial privacy law so banks and credit card companies must get your explicit permission — an 'opt-in' — before selling your financial data. Health information could no longer be sold for marketing. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers: anyone whose personal details are currently collected and sold. The bill targets the main fuels of identity theft — Social Security numbers displayed in public records, sold on websites, or printed on checks and licenses — and gives people a permanent, enforceable say over who may buy their information. People could sue violators for up to $500 per violation, tripled for willful conduct, and state attorneys general could sue on residents' behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Companies could not sell or share personally identifiable information with outside parties unless they first gave notice and an easy, permanent opt-out; violating it carried penalties up to $25,000 per violation.

Displaying, selling, or buying a Social Security number without the person's express written or electronic consent would become a federal crime, with civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation and $50,000 for a pattern of violations.

Government agencies could no longer print Social Security numbers on checks or on driver's licenses and vehicle registrations, and prisoners could not be given jobs exposing them to others' Social Security numbers.

Businesses could not refuse to sell you a good or service because you declined to hand over your Social Security number, with limited exceptions for credit checks, law enforcement, or fraud prevention.

Banks and other financial institutions would need your affirmative consent before selling your nonpublic personal financial information to outside companies, reversing the current opt-out default under Gramm-Leach-Bliley.
Selling or marketing protected health information would be prohibited for entities outside HIPAA's direct coverage, with an anti-retaliation provision for people who refuse consent.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers who buy and resell personal information, banks and credit card issuers that monetize customer records, marketers who purchase the data, and companies whose compliance costs (notices, opt-out systems, redacting public records) could be passed on in prices.

drawbacks.text: Title I would preempt state privacy laws covering marketing and sale of personal information, so in those areas the federal floor would replace any stricter state protections.
A 'safe harbor' would shield companies from liability if they follow self-regulatory guidelines written by industry seal programs, as long as the FTC approves them.

The Social Security number ban carves out broad exceptions for business-to-business, credit and background checks, mergers, and data matching, and lets the Attorney General write regulations defining what business uses remain permitted.
Consumers could not bring class actions over a business refusing service for withholding a Social Security number, and that restriction itself was set to expire after six years.

Compliance costs — notice systems, consent tracking, redacting Social Security numbers from records — would fall on businesses, and public-record restrictions on paper documents were left to Attorney General discretion after a cost-benefit review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — making it a crime to traffic in Social Security numbers and requiring consent before personal data is sold — directly addresses identity theft and unwanted data brokerage, and gives consumers private rights of action to enforce it. The weaknesses are real: the opt-out regime in Title I is weaker than the opt-in the bill applies to financial data, industry self-regulation could dilute it, federal preemption could override stronger state laws, and many business exceptions soften the Social Security number ban. On balance it was a substantial consumer privacy upgrade, though imperfectly designed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Privacy Act of 2005 in the Senate on January 24, 2005, and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
No senator cosponsored the bill during the two-year life of the 109th Congress.
The bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, banks, and marketers are better off: they kept the ability to collect, sell, and share Americans' personal, financial, and Social Security data without consent, unchanged, for another Congress. Consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; never acted
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 24, 2005 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no opposition is recorded in the action history; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill criminalizes selling or buying Social Security numbers without consent and restricts harvesting them from public records, attacking the core business of firms that resell personal data. These companies profit from practices the bill's own findings link to fraud and identity theft.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and other financial institutions
industries.note: Gramm-Leach-Bliley would be rewritten to require affirmative opt-in consent before selling customers' financial data, replacing today's opt-out default and eliminating a revenue stream built on customer records.

Companies could no longer sell or share customer names, addresses, phone numbers, and emails to nonaffiliated marketers without notice and a permanent opt-out, cutting off purchased lists and data-sharing for targeting.
Entities outside HIPAA — including life insurers and employers — could no longer buy or sell protected health information for marketing, closing a side market in medical data.

The bill preserves credit checks, background checks, and fraud prevention as exceptions, so their legitimate data flows continue; only sales of Social Security numbers to the general public would stop.
